Birth of Cain and Abel.</title> <div sID="gen174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv49"/><hi type="bold">1. Eve said, I have gotten a man from the Lord--</hi>that is, "by the help of the Lord"--an expression of pious gratitude--and she called him Cain, that is, "a possession," as if valued above everything else; while the arrival of another son reminding Eve of the misery she had entailed on her offspring, led to the name Abel, that is, either weakness, vanity (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.5">Psa 39:5</reference>), or grief, lamentation. entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 4
 
Ge 4:1-26. Birth of Cain and Abel.

1. Eve said, I have gotten a man from the Lord--that is, "by the help of the Lord"--an expression of pious gratitude--and she called him Cain, that is, "a possession," as if valued above everything else; while the arrival of another son reminding Eve of the misery she had entailed on her offspring, led to the name Abel, that is, either weakness, vanity (Psa 39:5), or grief, lamentation. Cain and Abel were probably twins; and it is thought that, at this early period, children were born in pairs (Ge 5:4) [Calvin].

Abel was a keeper of sheep--</hi>literally, "a feeder of a flock," which, in Oriental countries, always includes goats as well as sheep. Abel, though the younger, is mentioned first, probably on account of the pre-eminence of his religious character. <div eID="gen175" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2. Abel was a keeper of sheep--literally, "a feeder of a flock," which, in Oriental countries, always includes goats as well as sheep. Abel, though the younger, is mentioned first, probably on account of the pre-eminence of his religious character.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv51"/><div sID="gen176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv51"/><hi type="bold">3. in process of time--</hi>Hebrew, "at the end of days," probably on the Sabbath.<div eID="gen176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought ... an offering unto the Lord--</hi>Both manifested, by the very act of offering, their faith in the being of God and in His claims to their reverence and worship; and had the kind of offering been left to themselves, what more natural than that the one should bring "of the fruits of the ground," and that the other should bring "of the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof" [Ge 4:4]. <div eID="gen177" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
3. in process of time--Hebrew, "at the end of days," probably on the Sabbath.
 
brought ... an offering unto the Lord--Both manifested, by the very act of offering, their faith in the being of God and in His claims to their reverence and worship; and had the kind of offering been left to themselves, what more natural than that the one should bring "of the fruits of the ground," and that the other should bring "of the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof" [Ge 4:4].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv52"/><div sID="gen178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv52"/><hi type="bold">4. the Lord had respect unto Abel, not unto Cain, &c.--</hi>The words, "had respect to," signify in Hebrew,--"to look at any thing with a keen earnest glance," which has been translated, "kindle into a fire," so that the divine approval of Abel's offering was shown in its being consumed by fire (see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Ge 15:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.13.20">Jud 13:20</reference>). <div eID="gen178" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 4. the Lord had respect unto Abel, not unto Cain, &c.--The words, "had respect to," signify in Hebrew,--"to look at any thing with a keen earnest glance," which has been translated, "kindle into a fire," so that the divine approval of Abel's offering was shown in its being consumed by fire (see Ge 15:17; Jud 13:20).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv53"/><div sID="gen179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv53"/><hi type="bold">7. If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?--</hi>A better rendering is, "Shalt thou not have the excellency"? which is the true sense of the words referring to the high privileges and authority belonging to the first-born in patriarchal times.<div eID="gen179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin lieth at the door--</hi>sin, that is, a sin offering--a common meaning of the word in Scripture (as in <reference osisRef="Hos.4.8">Ho 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>). The purport of the divine rebuke to Cain was this, "Why art thou angry, as if unjustly treated? If thou doest well (that is, wert innocent and sinless) a thank offering would have been accepted as a token of thy dependence as a creature. But as thou doest not well (that is, art a sinner), a sin offering is necessary, by bringing which thou wouldest have met with acceptance and retained the honors of thy birthright." This language implies that previous instructions had been given as to the mode of worship; Abel offered through faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.4">He 11:4</reference>).<div eID="gen180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto thee shall be his desire--</hi>The high distinction conferred by priority of birth is described (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.29">Ge 27:29</reference>); and it was Cain's conviction, that this honor had been withdrawn from him, by the rejection of his sacrifice, and conferred on his younger brother--hence the secret flame of jealousy, which kindled into a settled hatred and fell revenge. <div eID="gen181" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
7. If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?--A better rendering is, "Shalt thou not have the excellency"? which is the true sense of the words referring to the high privileges and authority belonging to the first-born in patriarchal times.
 
sin lieth at the door--sin, that is, a sin offering--a common meaning of the word in Scripture (as in Ho 4:8; 2Co 5:21; He 9:28). The purport of the divine rebuke to Cain was this, "Why art thou angry, as if unjustly treated? If thou doest well (that is, wert innocent and sinless) a thank offering would have been accepted as a token of thy dependence as a creature. But as thou doest not well (that is, art a sinner), a sin offering is necessary, by bringing which thou wouldest have met with acceptance and retained the honors of thy birthright." This language implies that previous instructions had been given as to the mode of worship; Abel offered through faith (He 11:4).
 
unto thee shall be his desire--The high distinction conferred by priority of birth is described (Ge 27:29); and it was Cain's conviction, that this honor had been withdrawn from him, by the rejection of his sacrifice, and conferred on his younger brother--hence the secret flame of jealousy, which kindled into a settled hatred and fell revenge.

And Cain talked with Abel his brother--</hi>Under the guise of brotherly familiarity, he concealed his premeditated purpose till a convenient time and place occurred for the murder (<reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1Jo 3:12</reference>; Jude 11). <div eID="gen182" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. And Cain talked with Abel his brother--Under the guise of brotherly familiarity, he concealed his premeditated purpose till a convenient time and place occurred for the murder (1Jo 3:12; Jude 11).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv56"/><div sID="gen184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv56"/><hi type="bold">10. the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me--</hi>Cain, to lull suspicion, had probably been engaging in the solemnities of religion when he was challenged directly from the Shekinah itself. <div eID="gen184" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me--Cain, to lull suspicion, had probably been engaging in the solemnities of religion when he was challenged directly from the Shekinah itself.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv61"/><div sID="gen189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv61"/><hi type="bold">15. whosoever slayeth Cain--</hi>By a special act of divine forbearance, the life of Cain was to be spared in the then small state of the human race.<div eID="gen189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set a mark--</hi>not any visible mark or brand on his forehead, but some sign or token of assurance that his life would be preserved. This sign is thought by the best writers to have been a wild ferocity of aspect that rendered him an object of universal horror and avoidance. <div eID="gen190" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
15. whosoever slayeth Cain--By a special act of divine forbearance, the life of Cain was to be spared in the then small state of the human race.
 
set a mark--not any visible mark or brand on his forehead, but some sign or token of assurance that his life would be preserved. This sign is thought by the best writers to have been a wild ferocity of aspect that rendered him an object of universal horror and avoidance.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv62"/><div sID="gen191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv62"/><hi type="bold">16. presence of the Lord--</hi>the appointed place of worship at Eden. Leaving it, he not only severed himself from his relatives but forsook the ordinances of religion, probably casting off all fear of God from his eyes so that the last end of this man is worse than the first (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.45">Mt 12:45</reference>).<div eID="gen191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land of Nod--</hi>of flight or exile--thought by many to have been Arabia-Petræa--which was cursed to sterility on his account. <div eID="gen192" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
16. presence of the Lord--the appointed place of worship at Eden. Leaving it, he not only severed himself from his relatives but forsook the ordinances of religion, probably casting off all fear of God from his eyes so that the last end of this man is worse than the first (Mt 12:45).
 
land of Nod--of flight or exile--thought by many to have been Arabia-Petræa--which was cursed to sterility on his account.
